claim: Parkinson's disease is a progressive neuropathological disorder that belongs to the class of synucleinopathies.
source: Parkinson's disease is a progressive neuropathological disorder that belongs to the class of synucleinopathies, in which the protein alpha-synuclein is found at abnormally high concentrations in affected neurons.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about Parkinson's disease classification, representing established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: In synucleinopathies, the protein alpha-synuclein is found at abnormally high concentrations in affected neurons.
source: Parkinson's disease is a progressive neuropathological disorder that belongs to the class of synucleinopathies, in which the protein alpha-synuclein is found at abnormally high concentrations in affected neurons.
evidence: This statement describes a characteristic feature of synucleinopathies based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: The hallmark of Parkinson's disease are intracellular inclusions called Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites.
source: Its hallmark are intracellular inclusions called Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites.
evidence: This is a well-established characteristic of Parkinson's disease pathology.

claim: The structure of cytotoxic alpha-synuclein fibrils (residues 1–121) was determined by cryo-electron microscopy at a resolution of 3.4 Å.
source: We here report the structure of cytotoxic alpha-synuclein fibrils (residues 1–121), determined by cryo-electron microscopy at a resolution of 3.4 Å.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental cryo-EM data.

claim: Two protofilaments form a polar fibril composed of staggered β-strands in alpha-synuclein fibrils.
source: Two protofilaments form a polar fibril composed of staggered β-strands.
evidence: This structural finding is derived from the cryo-EM reconstruction data.

claim: The backbone of residues 38 to 95, including the fibril core and the non-amyloid component region, are well resolved in the EM map.
source: The backbone of residues 38 to 95, including the fibril core and the non-amyloid component region, are well resolved in the EM map.
evidence: This describes the quality and extent of the structural data obtained from cryo-EM.

claim: Residues 50–57, containing three of the mutation sites associated with familial synucleinopathies, form the interface between the two protofilaments.
source: Residues 50–57, containing three of the mutation sites associated with familial synucleinopathies, form the interface between the two protofilaments and contribute to fibril stability.
evidence: This structural observation is based on the cryo-EM structure and relates to known mutation sites.

claim: Residues 50–57 contribute to fibril stability.
source: Residues 50–57, containing three of the mutation sites associated with familial synucleinopathies, form the interface between the two protofilaments and contribute to fibril stability.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural position of these residues at the protofilament interface.

claim: A hydrophobic cleft at one end of the fibril may have implications for fibril elongation.
source: A hydrophobic cleft at one end of the fibril may have implications for fibril elongation, and invites for the design of molecules for diagnosis and treatment of synucleinopathies.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed structural feature.

claim: Spillantini et al. (1997) identified fibrils formed by the presynaptic protein alpha-synuclein as the main component of Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites.
source: Spillantini et al. (1997) identified fibrils formed by the presynaptic protein alpha-synuclein (α-Syn, 140 residues, ~14 kD) as the main component of these human brain inclusions (Spillantini et al., 1998; Spillantini et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Alpha-synuclein is a presynaptic protein of 140 residues and approximately 14 kD.
source: Spillantini et al. (1997) identified fibrils formed by the presynaptic protein alpha-synuclein (α-Syn, 140 residues, ~14 kD) as the main component of these human brain inclusions (Spillantini et al., 1998; Spillantini et al., 1997).
evidence: This is basic biochemical information about alpha-synuclein.

claim: Certain α-Syn fibril forms can seed LB-like and LN-like inclusions in cell culture.
source: Certain α-Syn fibril forms can seed LB-like and LN-like inclusions in cell culture and intra-neuronal aggregation of mouse α-Syn in vivo (Luk et al., 2009; Thakur et al., 2017; Volpicelli-Daley et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: Certain α-Syn fibril forms can seed intra-neuronal aggregation of mouse α-Syn in vivo.
source: Certain α-Syn fibril forms can seed LB-like and LN-like inclusions in cell culture and intra-neuronal aggregation of mouse α-Syn in vivo (Luk et al., 2009; Thakur et al., 2017; Volpicelli-Daley et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: Abnormal α-Syn produces neuronal cell inclusions and axonal spheroids.
source: In addition, abnormal α-Syn produces neuronal cell inclusions and axonal spheroids, as well as oligodendrocytic aggregates, known as glial cytoplasmic inclusions, found abundantly in Multiple System Atrophy (MSA) (Arima et al., 1998; Tu et al., 1998), which makes α-Syn fibrils an important target for the development of diagnostic tools and therapeutic strategies for PD and related synucleinopathies.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Abnormal α-Syn produces oligodendrocytic aggregates known as glial cytoplasmic inclusions found abundantly in Multiple System Atrophy (MSA).
source: In addition, abnormal α-Syn produces neuronal cell inclusions and axonal spheroids, as well as oligodendrocytic aggregates, known as glial cytoplasmic inclusions, found abundantly in Multiple System Atrophy (MSA) (Arima et al., 1998; Tu et al., 1998), which makes α-Syn fibrils an important target for the development of diagnostic tools and therapeutic strategies for PD and related synucleinopathies.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: α-Syn fibrils are an important target for the development of diagnostic tools and therapeutic strategies for PD and related synucleinopathies.
source: In addition, abnormal α-Syn produces neuronal cell inclusions and axonal spheroids, as well as oligodendrocytic aggregates, known as glial cytoplasmic inclusions, found abundantly in Multiple System Atrophy (MSA) (Arima et al., 1998; Tu et al., 1998), which makes α-Syn fibrils an important target for the development of diagnostic tools and therapeutic strategies for PD and related synucleinopathies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pathological role of α-Syn fibrils.

claim: Other forms of α-Syn besides fibrils might also be involved in neurodegeneration, such as an oligomeric α-Syn intermediate.
source: Despite α-Syn fibrils, other forms of α-Syn might also be involved in neurodegeneration, such as an oligomeric α-Syn intermediate (Danzer et al., 2007; Lashuel et al., 2002; Outeiro et al., 2008; Vicente Miranda et al., 2017; Villar-Piqué et al., 2016; Winner et al., 2011), or the process of fibril aggregation itself (Oueslati et al., 2010; Reynolds et al., 2017; Taschenberger et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The process of fibril aggregation itself might be involved in neurodegeneration.
source: Despite α-Syn fibrils, other forms of α-Syn might also be involved in neurodegeneration, such as an oligomeric α-Syn intermediate (Danzer et al., 2007; Lashuel et al., 2002; Outeiro et al., 2008; Vicente Miranda et al., 2017; Villar-Piqué et al., 2016; Winner et al., 2011), or the process of fibril aggregation itself (Oueslati et al., 2010; Reynolds et al., 2017; Taschenberger et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Fibrils of α-Syn show significant fibril strain polymorphism.
source: Fibrils of α-Syn show significant fibril strain polymorphism (Peelaerts et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Six known point mutations in the α-Syn gene (SNCA) are associated with familial forms of synucleinopathies: A30P, E46K, H50Q, G51D, A53E, and A53T.
source: Several factors point to α-Syn as an important player in the onset of PD: (i) six known point mutations in the α-Syn gene (SNCA) are associated with familial forms of synucleinopathies: A30P (Krüger et al., 1998), E46K (Zarranz et al., 2004), H50Q (Appel-Cresswell et al., 2013), G51D (Lesage et al., 2013), A53E (Pasanen et al., 2014), and A53T (Polymeropoulos et al., 1997);
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple prior studies identifying these mutations.

claim: Animal models suggest a role of α-Syn in the etiology of PD, Dementia with Lewy Bodies (DLB), and MSA.
source: (ii) animal models suggest a role of α-Syn in the etiology of PD, Dementia with Lewy Bodies (DLB), and MSA (Feany and Bender, 2000; Hashimoto et al., 2003; Periquet et al., 2007; Tyson et al., 2017);
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior animal model studies.

claim: Individuals with duplications or triplications of the α-Syn gene exhibit overexpression of α-Syn and develop PD.
source: (iii) individuals with duplications or triplications of the α-Syn gene exhibit overexpression of α-Syn and develop PD (Ibáñez et al., 2004; Singleton et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior genetic studies.

claim: β-synuclein (β-Syn) and γ-synuclein (γ-Syn) are two related proteins with sequence homology to α-Syn.
source: Two related proteins, β-synuclein (β-Syn) and γ-synuclein (γ-Syn), with sequence homology to α-Syn, have been described (Clayton and George, 1998; Jakes et al., 1994; Stefanis, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: β-Syn and α-Syn share the greatest aminoacid sequence homology.
source: β-Syn and α-Syn share the greatest aminoacid sequence homology, with β-Syn lacking 12 amino acids (residues 71 to 82) within the non-amyloid component region (NAC; residues 61–95 in α-Syn) (Giasson et al., 2001; Uéda et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: β-Syn lacks 12 amino acids (residues 71 to 82) within the non-amyloid component region (NAC; residues 61–95 in α-Syn).
source: β-Syn and α-Syn share the greatest aminoacid sequence homology, with β-Syn lacking 12 amino acids (residues 71 to 82) within the non-amyloid component region (NAC; residues 61–95 in α-Syn) (Giasson et al., 2001; Uéda et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: In synucleins, regions with the highest homologies are located in the structurally heterogeneous, amino-terminal half (residues 10–84 in α-Syn) composed of 5 to 6 imperfect repeats with the consensus sequence KTKEGV.
source: In synucleins, regions with the highest homologies are located in the structurally heterogeneous, amino-terminal half (residues 10–84 in α-Syn) composed of 5 to 6 imperfect repeats with the consensus sequence KTKEGV (Der-Sarkissian et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: The carboxyl terminus of synucleins is highly negatively charged and unstructured.
source: In contrast, the carboxyl terminus is highly negatively charged and unstructured (Chen et al., 2007; Vilar et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Post-translational modifications of α-Syn include phosphorylation, acetylation, ubiquitination, and C-terminal truncation.
source: A number of post-translational modifications have been described for α-Syn including phosphorylation (Anderson et al., 2006; Fujiwara et al., 2002; Paleologou et al., 2010), acetylation (Iyer et al., 2016; Maltsev et al., 2012), ubiquitination (Hasegawa et al., 2002), and C-terminal truncation (Anderson et al., 2006; Crowther et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: C-terminal truncation of α-Syn occurs normally in vivo under physiological conditions.
source: C-terminal truncation of α-Syn occurs normally in vivo, under physiological conditions and it has been shown to promote fibrillization (Crowther et al., 1998; Li et al., 2005; Liu et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: C-terminal truncation of α-Syn has been shown to promote fibrillization.
source: C-terminal truncation of α-Syn occurs normally in vivo, under physiological conditions and it has been shown to promote fibrillization (Crowther et al., 1998; Li et al., 2005; Liu et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Truncated forms of α-Syn play a role in inducing Lewy body formation.
source: In turn, truncated forms of α-Syn play a role in inducing Lewy body formation (Dufty et al., 2007; Li et al., 2005; Prasad et al., 2012), suggesting that truncation by proteolysis may be important in the pathological process.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Truncation by proteolysis may be important in the pathological process of synucleinopathies.
source: In turn, truncated forms of α-Syn play a role in inducing Lewy body formation (Dufty et al., 2007; Li et al., 2005; Prasad et al., 2012), suggesting that truncation by proteolysis may be important in the pathological process.
evidence: This is an inference based on the role of truncated forms in Lewy body formation.

claim: Activation of the inflammasome and caspase-1 leads to the production of an α-Syn fragment truncated at aspartic acid 121 (D121).
source: In vivo studies investigating α-Syn aggregation demonstrated that activation of the inflammasome and more specifically caspase-1, the enzymatic component of the inflammasome, leads to the production of an α-Syn fragment truncated at aspartic acid 121 (D121) (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: α-Syn(1-121) aggregates more rapidly than full-length α-Syn (including disease-associated mutants).
source: This C-terminally-truncated α-Syn form (α-Syn(1-121)) aggregates more rapidly than full-length α-Syn (including disease-associated mutants), and its production is associated with cell toxicity.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2016 in the preceding sentence.

claim: Production of α-Syn(1-121) is associated with cell toxicity.
source: This C-terminally-truncated α-Syn form (α-Syn(1-121)) aggregates more rapidly than full-length α-Syn (including disease-associated mutants), and its production is associated with cell toxicity.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2016 in the preceding sentence.

claim: VX-765 is a pro-drug that produces a specific inhibitor of caspase-1 in vivo.
source: Furthermore, the use of VX-765, a pro-drug that produces a specific inhibitor of caspase-1 in vivo (Wannamaker et al., 2007), improved survival of a neuronal cell model of PD (Wang et al., 2016), and reduced neurodegeneration in a transgenic mouse model of MSA (Bassil et al., 2016), suggesting an important role of α-Syn(1-121) in cellular toxicity in both, cell cultures as well as a mouse model.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: VX-765 improved survival of a neuronal cell model of PD.
source: Furthermore, the use of VX-765, a pro-drug that produces a specific inhibitor of caspase-1 in vivo (Wannamaker et al., 2007), improved survival of a neuronal cell model of PD (Wang et al., 2016), and reduced neurodegeneration in a transgenic mouse model of MSA (Bassil et al., 2016), suggesting an important role of α-Syn(1-121) in cellular toxicity in both, cell cultures as well as a mouse model.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: VX-765 reduced neurodegeneration in a transgenic mouse model of MSA.
source: Furthermore, the use of VX-765, a pro-drug that produces a specific inhibitor of caspase-1 in vivo (Wannamaker et al., 2007), improved survival of a neuronal cell model of PD (Wang et al., 2016), and reduced neurodegeneration in a transgenic mouse model of MSA (Bassil et al., 2016), suggesting an important role of α-Syn(1-121) in cellular toxicity in both, cell cultures as well as a mouse model.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: α-Syn(1-121) plays an important role in cellular toxicity in both cell cultures and a mouse model.
source: Furthermore, the use of VX-765, a pro-drug that produces a specific inhibitor of caspase-1 in vivo (Wannamaker et al., 2007), improved survival of a neuronal cell model of PD (Wang et al., 2016), and reduced neurodegeneration in a transgenic mouse model of MSA (Bassil et al., 2016), suggesting an important role of α-Syn(1-121) in cellular toxicity in both, cell cultures as well as a mouse model.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effects of VX-765 in the cited studies.

claim: High resolution structures of α-Syn fibrils are limited to a micro-electron diffraction (microED) study of two small segments of the protein and a solid-state NMR structure obtained from ~5 nm diameter single protofilaments.
source: To this date, high resolution structures of α-Syn fibrils are limited to the results of a micro-electron diffraction (microED) study of two small segments of the protein (Rodriguez et al., 2015) and a solid-state NMR structure obtained from ~5 nm diameter, single protofilaments (Tuttle et al., 2016), in addition to solid state NMR studies at the secondary structure level (Bousset et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2009; Vilar et al., 2008), and X-ray diffraction studies of shorter segments of α-Syn (Li et al., 2014), or α-Syn bound to other molecules (De Genst et al., 2010; Gruschus et al., 2013; Rao et al., 2010; Ulmer et al., 2005; Xie et al., 2010; Yagi-Utsumi et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claim: The atomic structure of α-Syn(1-121) fibrils allows conclusions about the organization of α-Syn fibrils at near-atomic resolution.
source: Here, we report the atomic structure of α-Syn(1-121) fibrils determined by cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). The structure allows conclusions about the organization of α-Syn fibrils at near-atomic resolution, suggest mechanisms for fibril formation and growth, and allows conclusions on fibril stability.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure determined in this study.

claim: The atomic structure of α-Syn(1-121) fibrils suggests mechanisms for fibril formation and growth.
source: Here, we report the atomic structure of α-Syn(1-121) fibrils determined by cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). The structure allows conclusions about the organization of α-Syn fibrils at near-atomic resolution, suggest mechanisms for fibril formation and growth, and allows conclusions on fibril stability.
evidence: This is based on inferences from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The atomic structure of α-Syn(1-121) fibrils allows conclusions on fibril stability.
source: Here, we report the atomic structure of α-Syn(1-121) fibrils determined by cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). The structure allows conclusions about the organization of α-Syn fibrils at near-atomic resolution, suggest mechanisms for fibril formation and growth, and allows conclusions on fibril stability.
evidence: This is based on inferences from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The fibrils formed by α-Syn(1-121) were straight, between 20 and 500 nm long and had consistent diameters of 10 nm.
source: The fibrils formed by α-Syn(1-121) were straight, between 20 and 500 nm long and the only ones of consistent diameters of 10 nm (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is based on negative stain TEM observations.

claim: Helical image processing of recorded cryo-EM movies produced a 3D reconstruction of the α-Syn(1-121) fibril at an overall resolution of 3.4 Å.
source: Helical image processing of recorded cryo-EM movies produced a 3D reconstruction of the α-Syn(1-121) fibril at an overall resolution of 3.4 Å (Figure 1C and D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 2, and Video 1).
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM data processing.

claim: The 3D map shows that fibrils are formed by two protofilaments, each of 5 nm in diameter.
source: Our 3D map shows that fibrils are formed by two protofilaments, each of 5 nm in diameter (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM reconstruction.

claim: The two protofilaments lack C2 symmetry but are related by an approximate 21 screw symmetry.
source: These lack C2 symmetry, but are related by an approximate 21 screw symmetry, akin to the symmetry exhibited by the paired helical filaments of tau (Fitzpatrick et al., 2017) and by amyloid-ß(1-42) filaments (Gremer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure and comparison with other amyloid structures.

claim: α-Syn(1-121) fibrils are polar, meaning that both protofibrils are aligned into the same direction.
source: α-Syn(1-121) fibrils are therefore polar, meaning that both protofibrils are aligned into the same direction.
evidence: This is inferred from the approximate 21 screw symmetry observed in the structure.

claim: The position of a given ß-sheet in a protofilament is produced by the rotation of 179.5° of one sheet around its axis (helical twist), followed by a vertical translation of 2.45 Å (helical rise).
source: The position of a given ß-sheet in a protofilament is produced by the rotation of 179.5° of one sheet around its axis (helical twist), followed by a vertical translation of 2.45 Å (helical rise).
evidence: This is based on the helical parameters determined from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The ß-sheet arrangement results in a spacing of 4.9 Å between α-Syn subunits in successive rungs of a single protofilament.
source: This ß-sheet arrangement results in a spacing of 4.9 Å between α-Syn subunits in successive rungs of a single protofilament (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The quality of the EM map allowed an atomic model of the region between residues L38 and V95 to be built.
source: The quality of the EM map allowed an atomic model of the region between residues L38 and V95 to be built.
evidence: This is based on the resolution and quality of the cryo-EM map.

claim: Each α-Syn(1-121) molecule comprises eight in-register parallel β-strands.
source: Each α-Syn(1-121) molecule comprises eight in-register parallel β-strands (i.e. residues 42–46 (β1), 48–49 (β2), 52–57 (β3), 59–66 (β4), 69–72 (β5), 77–82 (β6), 89–92 (β7), and 94-(~102) (β8)), which are interrupted by glycine residues (i.e. G41 before β1, G47 between β1 and β2, G51 between β2 and β3, G67 and G68 between β4 and β5, G73 between β5 and β6, G84 and G86 between β6 and β7, and G93 between β7 and β8) or an arch (i.e. E57-K58 between β3 and β4) (Figure 1A,F and G).
evidence: This is based on the atomic model built from the cryo-EM map.

claim: The β-strands β2-β7 wind around a hydrophobic intra-molecular core composed of only alanine and valine residues and one isoleucine.
source: The β-strands β2-β7 wind around a hydrophobic intra-molecular core composed of only alanine and valine residues and one isoleucine (i.e. V48, V49, V52, A53, V55, V63, A69, V70, V71, V74, A76, V77, A78, I88, A89, A90, A91).
evidence: This is based on the atomic model and structural analysis.

claim: The hydrophobic clusters are likely to contribute to the stability of the protofilament.
source: Considering that these hydrophobic clusters are maintained along the fibril, they are likely to contribute to the stability of the protofilament.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation of hydrophobic clusters.

claim: The hydrophobic core is surrounded by two hydrophilic regions.
source: The hydrophobic core is surrounded by two hydrophilic regions (i.e. (i): Q79, T81, and (ii): T72, T75, T54, T59, and E61) both still within the core of the structure (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on the atomic model and structural analysis.

claim: Most of the hydrophilic side chains form side chain hydrogen bond ladders.
source: While most of these side chains form so-called side chain hydrogen bond ladders (Nelson et al., 2005; Riek, 2017), the second hydrophilic region comprising four threonine residues and a negatively charged glutamic acid side chain surrounds a tunnel filled with some ordered molecules of unknown nature, as evidenced by an additional density (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and comparison with known structural motifs.

claim: The second hydrophilic region surrounds a tunnel filled with some ordered molecules of unknown nature.
source: While most of these side chains form so-called side chain hydrogen bond ladders (Nelson et al., 2005; Riek, 2017), the second hydrophilic region comprising four threonine residues and a negatively charged glutamic acid side chain surrounds a tunnel filled with some ordered molecules of unknown nature, as evidenced by an additional density (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is based on observation of additional density in the cryo-EM map.

claim: The first 37 N-terminal residues and the last ~20 C-terminal residues of α-Syn(1-121) are not visible in the 3D reconstruction, indicating a disordered structure.
source: The less well defined β1 and β8 strands are attached to the core, while the first 37 N-terminal residues and the last ~20 C-terminal residues of α-Syn(1-121) are not visible in the 3D reconstruction (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), indicating a disordered structure in line with quenched hydrogen/deuterium exchange – solution-state NMR (H/D exchange NMR) and limited proteolysis (Vilar et al., 2008), which showed these terminal segments to be unprotected in nature.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM map and comparison with prior NMR and proteolysis studies.

claim: Approximately 40 residues of both the N- and C-terminal ends of full-length human α-Syn are flexible and surround the structured core of the fibril with a dense mesh of disordered tails.
source: Together with our results, this suggests that approximately 40 residues of both the N- and C-terminal ends of full-length human α-Syn are flexible, and surround the structured core of the fibril with a dense mesh of disordered tails, similar to the 'fuzzy coat' recently described in the cryo-EM tau structure (Fitzpatrick et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the cryo-EM structure and comparison with the tau structure.

claim: Two β-sheets (one from each protofilament) interact at the fibril core via a hydrophobic steric zipper-geometry comprised of β-strand β3 (residues G51-A56).
source: Two β-sheets (one from each protofilament) interact at the fibril core via a hydrophobic steric zipper-geometry comprised of β-strand β3 (i.e. residues G51-A56).
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Two α-Syn molecules per fibril layer are stacked along the fibril axis.
source: As a consequence, two α-Syn molecules per fibril layer are stacked along the fibril axis (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The side chains of residues A53 and V55 form the inter-molecular surface contributing to the interface between the two protofilaments.
source: The side chains of residues A53 and V55 form the inter-molecular surface contributing to the interface between the two protofilaments, which is further stabilized by a surface-exposed salt bridge between E57 and H50 that might be sensitive to pH, as an unprotected histidine has a pK of ~6.2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3H).
evidence: This is based on the atomic model and structural analysis.

claim: The interface between the two protofilaments is further stabilized by a surface-exposed salt bridge between E57 and H50 that might be sensitive to pH.
source: The side chains of residues A53 and V55 form the inter-molecular surface contributing to the interface between the two protofilaments, which is further stabilized by a surface-exposed salt bridge between E57 and H50 that might be sensitive to pH, as an unprotected histidine has a pK of ~6.2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3H).
evidence: This is based on the atomic model and knowledge of histidine pK values.

claim: The same structure with a steric zipper topology was found in micro-crystals of the peptide comprising residues G47-A56.
source: The same structure with a steric zipper topology was found in micro-crystals of the peptide comprising residues G47-A56 (Rodriguez et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior microED study.

claim: The β-strand β6 is aligned with a neighboring molecule but shifted by one monomer along the fibril axis.
source: Interestingly, the β-strand β6 that is sandwiched between β-strands β2/β3 and β7 is also aligned with a neighboring molecule but shifted by one monomer along the fibril axis, as shown in Figure 1G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Hetero and homo steric zippers are both present in the 3D structure.
source: Thus, hetero and homo steric zippers are both present in the 3D structure.
evidence: This is based on the structural analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The homo steric zipper at the inter-molecular interface has an extensive and well-packed β-strand interface, forming a very densely packed fibril.
source: Of these, the homo steric zipper at the inter-molecular interface has an extensive and well-packed β-strand interface, forming a very densely packed fibril.
evidence: This is based on the structural analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The stacking generates an asymmetric fibril with two distinct ends.
source: This stacking generates an asymmetric fibril with two distinct ends.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural arrangement observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The hydrophobic core of the fibril is composed of β-strands that interact with each other in a half-stacked zipper topology.
source: Furthermore, the hydrophobic core of the fibril is composed of β-strands that interact with each other in a half-stacked zipper topology, contrasting with the hydrophilic core comprised of β-strands β4 and β5, which are non-stacked (Figure 1G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the structural analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The hydrophilic core comprised of β-strands β4 and β5 are non-stacked.
source: Furthermore, the hydrophobic core of the fibril is composed of β-strands that interact with each other in a half-stacked zipper topology, contrasting with the hydrophilic core comprised of β-strands β4 and β5, which are non-stacked (Figure 1G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the structural analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The region including residues 62–67 at the beginning of the NAC region has a pronounced lack of stacking interactions.
source: The latter confirms previous results from site-directed spin labeling experiments, which show that the region including residues 62–67 at the beginning of the NAC region, has a pronounced lack of stacking interactions (Chen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure and comparison with prior spin labeling experiments.

claim: The outer surface of the ordered region of the fibrils is mostly hydrophilic, with a few exceptions.
source: The outer surface of the ordered region of the fibrils is mostly hydrophilic, with a few exceptions (i.e. L38, V40, V82, A85, A90, F94, V95) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on the atomic model and hydrophobicity analysis.

claim: The surface of the fibrils has two highly hydrophobic regions formed by residues L38 and V40, and by residues F94 and V95.
source: If we ignore the influence of the non-polar alanine residues due to the small size of their side chains, the surface of the fibrils has two highly hydrophobic regions formed by residues L38 and V40, and by residues F94 and V95.
evidence: This is based on the atomic model and hydrophobicity analysis.

claim: The side chains of E46 and K80 form a salt bridge on the surface of the fibrils.
source: Other interesting properties of the surface are the salt bridge formed by the side chains of E46 and K80 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3G) and the rather highly positive clustering of K43, K45, K58, H50 that requests the binding of a counter-ion, as it is supported by an observed density (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is based on the atomic model and structural analysis.

claim: There is a highly positive clustering of K43, K45, K58, H50 that requests the binding of a counter-ion.
source: Other interesting properties of the surface are the salt bridge formed by the side chains of E46 and K80 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3G) and the rather highly positive clustering of K43, K45, K58, H50 that requests the binding of a counter-ion, as it is supported by an observed density (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is based on the atomic model and observation of additional density in the cryo-EM map.

claim: All familial mutations except A30P are located in the heart of the core of the fibril structure.
source: Six familial mutations in α-Syn are known to be associated with PD and other synucleinopathies (i.e. A30P, E46K, H50Q, G51D, A53E, and A53T). Of these, all but A30P are located in the heart of the core of the fibril structure presented here (Figure 1A and E).
evidence: This is based on mapping the mutation sites onto the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The mutation of E46 to lysine in an E46K mutant would induce a charge repulsion between β-strands β1 and β6, likely destabilizing this α-Syn fibril structure.
source: E46 forms a salt bridge with K80 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3G). The mutation of the glutamic acid E46 to a positively charged lysine in an E46K mutant would thus induce a charge repulsion between β-strands β1 and β6, likely destabilizing this α-Syn fibril structure (Tuttle et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural role of E46 and basic electrostatic principles.

claim: The familial PD/DLB-causing mutation E46K was found to enhance phosphorylation in mice.
source: The familial PD/DLB-causing mutation E46K was found to enhance phosphorylation in mice (Mbefo et al., 2015), and its toxic effect was increased by the triple-K mutation (E35K, E46K, E61K) in neuronal cells (Dettmer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The toxic effect of E46K was increased by the triple-K mutation (E35K, E46K, E61K) in neuronal cells.
source: The familial PD/DLB-causing mutation E46K was found to enhance phosphorylation in mice (Mbefo et al., 2015), and its toxic effect was increased by the triple-K mutation (E35K, E46K, E61K) in neuronal cells (Dettmer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: H50, G51 and A53 are all involved in the inter-molecular contact between the two β-sheets from adjacent protofilaments at the core of α-Syn(1-121) fibrils.
source: Our 3D map suggests structural contributions of some familial mutations to fibril stability, since H50, G51 and A53 are all involved in the inter-molecular contact between the two β-sheets from adjacent protofilaments at the core of the here studied α-Syn(1-121) fibrils.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Mutation of H50 to glutamine in the H50Q mutant would likely interfere with the salt bridge established between residues E57 and H50.
source: Mutation of the positively charged histidine 50 into a polar, uncharged glutamine in the H50Q mutant would likely interfere with the salt bridge established between residues E57 and H50 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3H).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural role of H50 and the chemical properties of glutamine.

claim: Adding a negatively charged aspartic acid in mutant G51D would likely disrupt the steric zipper interaction between the two protofibrils.
source: Adding to the absent side-chain of glycine 51 a negatively charged aspartic acid in mutant G51D, or transforming the small side-chain of alanine A53 into a larger threonine in mutant A53T, would likely disrupt the steric zipper interaction between the two protofibrils, whereby the A53T mutation would in addition change the highly hydrophobic surface at the zipper to partly hydrophilic one.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural role of G51 and the chemical properties of aspartic acid.

claim: Transforming A53 into threonine in mutant A53T would likely disrupt the steric zipper interaction between the two protofibrils.
source: Adding to the absent side-chain of glycine 51 a negatively charged aspartic acid in mutant G51D, or transforming the small side-chain of alanine A53 into a larger threonine in mutant A53T, would likely disrupt the steric zipper interaction between the two protofibrils, whereby the A53T mutation would in addition change the highly hydrophobic surface at the zipper to partly hydrophilic one.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural role of A53 and the chemical properties of threonine.

claim: The A53T mutation would change the highly hydrophobic surface at the zipper to partly hydrophilic one.
source: Adding to the absent side-chain of glycine 51 a negatively charged aspartic acid in mutant G51D, or transforming the small side-chain of alanine A53 into a larger threonine in mutant A53T, would likely disrupt the steric zipper interaction between the two protofibrils, whereby the A53T mutation would in addition change the highly hydrophobic surface at the zipper to partly hydrophilic one.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural role of A53 and the chemical properties of threonine.

claim: A53 is part of a hydrophobic pocket that defines the interaction of protofilaments and likely contributes to fibril stability.
source: In our α-Syn(1-121) fibril structure, A53 is part of a hydrophobic pocket that defines the interaction of protofilaments and likely contributes to fibril stability as the hydrophobic interactions exist along the fibril axis.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure and inference about the role of hydrophobic interactions.

claim: Mutations at the core of this α-Syn fibril would compromise the formation of the structure.
source: Mutations at the core of this α-Syn fibril would compromise the formation of the structure presented here.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural importance of the core residues.

claim: A different fibril structure (fibril strain) could be formed from α-Syn containing familial PD mutations.
source: This suggests that a different fibril structure (i.e. fibril strain) could be formed from α-Syn containing the above discussed familial PD mutations.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural analysis of mutation sites.

claim: Non-functional hydrophobic surface patches, a hydrophilic tunnel, and a positively charged side chain arrangement are not found in functional amyloid structures such as that of HET-s.
source: Several features of our structure, such as non-functional hydrophobic surface patches (Figure 3), a hydrophilic tunnel (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D), and a positively charged side chain arrangement like the one comprised of residues K43, K45, K58, H50 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C) are not found in functional amyloid structures such as that of HET-s (Wasmer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on comparison with the structure of HET-s.

claim: Similar structural characteristics have been observed for pathological tau filaments obtained from Alzheimer's disease brains.
source: However, similar structural characteristics have been previously observed for pathological tau filaments obtained from Alzheimer's disease brains where (i): lysine and tyrosine residues play a similarly stabilizing role in the interface region of two protofilaments of the straight filaments (SF), and (ii): the area in the center of the protofilaments is dominated by hydrophilic residues (Fitzpatrick et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study on tau filaments.

claim: Folding to form the amyloid fibril structure is dictated by the need to bury the maximum number of hydrophobic side-chains as efficiently as possible.
source: It is plausible that these structural features might arise because folding to form the amyloid fibril structure is dictated by the need to bury the maximum number of hydrophobic side-chains as efficiently as possible, as is also the case for the Aβ(1-42) amyloid fibrils (Gremer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculation based on general principles of protein folding and comparison with Aβ fibrils.

claim: The artificial mutant E57K was designed to interfere with amyloid fibril formation.
source: The presence of a positive lysine side chain at this position in the E57K mutant would significantly interfere with the formation of the interface and even the amyloid fibril (Winner et al., 2011). Indeed, this mutant was designed in a successful structure-based attempt to interfere with amyloid fibril formation (at least under some conditions) (Winner et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: The E57K mutant formed a significant amount of oligomers and was highly toxic in a lentivirus-rat system and in a transgenic mouse model.
source: Furthermore, both in a lentivirus-rat system as well as in a transgenic mouse model, the E57K mutant formed a significant amount of oligomers and was highly toxic, resulting in a large decay of TH-sensitive neurons in the substantia nigra of rats and a motor phenotype reminiscent of PD in mice (Winner et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: The E57K mutant can be regarded as a 'familial PD-like' mutation from both the in vivo and the structure/mechanism-based point of view.
source: Thus, the artificial mutant E57K can be regarded as a 'familial PD-like' mutation both from the in vivo and from the structure/mechanism-based point of view.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of the E57K mutant.

claim: Full-length α-Syn subunits in a fibril studied by NMR were found to be in a roughly similar secondary structure arrangement as in the α-Syn(1-121) structure.
source: Full-length α-Syn subunits in a fibril studied by NMR ([Tuttle et al., 2016], PDB 2N0A) were found to be in a roughly similar secondary structure arrangement as in the here reported structure of α-Syn(1-121) (Figure 4A), even though the primary structure and the side-chain interactions of our here reported structure are very different from the NMR structure.
evidence: This is based on comparison with the NMR structure.

claim: The primary structure and the side-chain interactions of the cryo-EM structure are very different from the NMR structure.
source: Full-length α-Syn subunits in a fibril studied by NMR ([Tuttle et al., 2016], PDB 2N0A) were found to be in a roughly similar secondary structure arrangement as in the here reported structure of α-Syn(1-121) (Figure 4A), even though the primary structure and the side-chain interactions of our here reported structure are very different from the NMR structure.
evidence: This is based on comparison with the NMR structure.

claim: The fibrils used for the NMR study were only approximately 5 nm wide, which corresponds to the diameter of a single protofilament.
source: Most importantly, the fibrils used for the NMR study were only approximately 5 nm wide, which corresponds to the diameter of a single protofilament.
evidence: This is based on comparison with the NMR study.

claim: The larger diameter of the cryo-EM fibrils (10 nm) results from the interaction between two protofilaments.
source: The larger diameter of our fibrils, 10 nm, results from the interaction between two protofilaments, which allowed us to hypothesize on the nature of α-Syn(1-121) protofilament interactions.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Fibrils of 5 to 10 nm in diameter have been found in substantia nigra samples from the brain of PD patients, cingulate cortex of patients with DLB, cerebral cortex of PD patients, and in-vitro aggregated samples.
source: Fibrils of 5 to 10 nm in diameter found in substantia nigra samples from the brain of PD patients, (Crowther et al., 2000), cingulate cortex of patients with DLB (Spillantini et al., 1998), cerebral cortex of PD patients (Kosaka et al., 1976), and in-vitro aggregated samples (Bousset et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Crowther et al. (2000) suggested that the 10 nm filaments are the result of the interaction between 5 nm protofilaments.
source: Crowther et al. (2000) had already suggested that the 10 nm filaments are the result of the interaction between 5 nm protofilaments.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: In the cryo-EM structure, residue A53 faces the interface between the two protofibrils and thereby likely contributes to fibril stability.
source: An important difference between our here reported structure and the NMR structure reported by Tuttle et al. (2016) is the orientation of residue A53. The mutation A53T is associated with early onset PD. In our structure, residue A53 faces the interface between the two protofibrils and thereby likely contributes to fibril stability.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure and inference about the role of A53.

claim: In the NMR structure, A53 points towards the hydrophobic core of the one observed individual protofilament.
source: In contrast, Tuttle et al. (2016) reported in their NMR structure A53 to point towards the hydrophobic core of the one observed individual protofilament, which may explain the lack of 10 nm fibrils in their sample.
evidence: This is based on comparison with the NMR structure.

claim: The NMR study by Tuttle et al. (2016) showed a significant disagreement among the ten lowest-energy NMR structures for residues 51–67, indicating a lower confidence for those residues in the NMR structure.
source: However, it is also noted here that the NMR study by Tuttle et al. (2016) showed a significant disagreement among the ten lowest-energy NMR structures for residues 51–67 [Figure 3d in Tuttle et al. (2016)], indicating a lower confidence for those residues in the NMR structure.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the NMR study.

claim: S87 is one of several phosphorylation sites in α-Syn, in addition to Y125, S129, Y133 and Y135.
source: Our structure includes a serine residue at position 87 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E), which is one of the several phosphorylation sites in α-Syn, in addition to Y125, S129, Y133 and Y135 (Oueslati et al., 2012; Paleologou et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: S87 is the only phosphorylation site located within the NAC region.
source: S87 is the only phosphorylation site located within the NAC region.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of the NAC region boundaries and phosphorylation sites.

claim: In the cryo-EM structure, S87 faces the outside of the fibril and hence remains accessible for disease-associated modification in α-Syn fibrils.
source: However, in our cryo-EM structure, S87 faces the outside of the fibril and hence remains accessible for disease-associated modification in α-Syn fibrils.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure and inference about accessibility.

claim: The arrangement of G47 and A78 favors the interaction between residues E46 and K80 and allows them to form a stable salt bridge between two consecutive α-Syn monomers.
source: We also observed the arrangement of G47 and A78 described by Tuttle et al. (2016), which was proposed to favor the interaction between residues E46 and K80 and allow them to form a stable salt bridge between two consecutive α-Syn monomers (Figure 1—figure supplement 3G).
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure and comparison with the NMR study.

claim: The conservation of the geometry adopted by G47 and A78 confirms their role in facilitating backbone-backbone interactions.
source: The conservation of the geometry adopted by these residues confirms their role in facilitating backbone-backbone interactions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural conservation observed.

claim: Residues A69 and G93 (and likely G68) help to stabilize the distal loop in a protofilament.
source: In addition, our structure also confirms that residues A69 and G93 (and likely G68) help to stabilize the distal loop in a protofilament (Figure 1—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure.

claim: A microED structure proposed that residue 53 forms the hydrophobic core within a protofilament.
source: A microED structure obtained from crystals produced from a 10-residue peptide simulating the core of α-Syn fibrils (PreNAC, from 47 to 56; Figure 4B) and including a threonine instead of an alanine at position 53 (i.e. A53T), also proposed that residue 53 forms the hydrophobic core within a protofilament (Rodriguez et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior microED study.

claim: The microED model suggested that the interaction between adjacent protofilaments would occur through residues 68 to 78 (NACore).
source: In addition, the microED model suggested that the interaction between adjacent protofilaments would occur through residues 68 to 78 (referred to as NACore) (Rodriguez et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior microED study.

claim: The cryo-EM structure reveals that the PreNAC is responsible for the interaction between protofilaments.
source: However, their short peptides did not include most residues responsible for the α-Syn monomer topology that we observed. Instead, our cryo-EM structure reveals that the PreNAC is responsible for the interaction between protofilaments, and places the NACore at the very center (i.e.the core) of a single protofilament.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure and comparison with the microED model.

claim: The cryo-EM structure places the NACore at the very center (the core) of a single protofilament.
source: However, their short peptides did not include most residues responsible for the α-Syn monomer topology that we observed. Instead, our cryo-EM structure reveals that the PreNAC is responsible for the interaction between protofilaments, and places the NACore at the very center (i.e.the core) of a single protofilament.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure and comparison with the microED model.

claim: The two ends of the fibrils are distinct, suggesting an end-dependent growth of the fibrils.
source: Because two different stacking modes are present (i.e. the half-stack at the intermolecular interface and the stacking of β-strand β6), the two ends of the fibrils are distinct, suggesting an end-dependent growth of the fibrils, as documented and also suggested for other amyloids (Lührs et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural asymmetry and comparison with other amyloids.

claim: One end of the fibril includes a hydrophobic cleft formed between β-strands β2/β3 on one side and β7 on the other side, providing a hydrophobic entry point for the next incoming molecule.
source: One end of the fibril includes a hydrophobic cleft formed between β-strands β2/ β3 on one side and β7 on the other side (residues V49, V52, A88, I89), providing a hydrophobic entry point for the next incoming molecule, with the matching segment consisting of 5 hydrophobic residues (V74-V82, Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure and inference about fibril elongation.

claim: The initial binding event of fibril elongation might be a hydrophobic interaction involving residues V74-V82.
source: This suggests that the initial binding event of fibril elongation might be a hydrophobic interaction involving residues V74-V82.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural observation of the hydrophobic cleft.

claim: The peptide segment V74-V82 is the central part of the NAC region and strong experimental evidence suggests that it is critical for fibril formation.
source: This peptide segment is the central part of the NAC region and strong experimental evidence suggests that it is critical for fibril formation (Giasson et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: β-synuclein, which lacks residues V74 to V82, is incapable of forming fibrils.
source: In addition, it has been shown that β-synuclein, which lacks residues V74 to V82, is incapable of forming fibrils (Giasson et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: A small molecule binding into the hydrophobic cleft could be a potent fibril elongation inhibitor or tracer.
source: It is intriguing to speculate that a small molecule binding into this hydrophobic cleft could be a potent fibril elongation inhibitor or tracer, with the potential to be applied in PD and other synucleinopathies.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural observation of the hydrophobic cleft.

claim: The inter-molecular stacking may play a role in fibril elongation.
source: Finally, the inter-molecular stacking may also play a role in fibril elongation, since the zipper interaction is of hydrophobic nature.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural observation of the steric zipper.

claim: Fibril growth likely alternates between the two protofilament structures at the level of monomer addition.
source: Furthermore, it is likely that fibril growth alternates between the two protofilament structures at the level of monomer addition.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural asymmetry of the fibril.

claim: Failure of alternating growth may result in the growth of a single protofilament with little stability, yielding a dynamic on- and off-binding of monomers and larger oligomers.
source: Failure thereof may result in the growth of a single protofilament with little stability, yielding a dynamic on- and off-binding of monomers and larger oligomers, which has been observed for other amyloid fibril systems (Carulla et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a speculation based on comparison with other amyloid systems.

claim: The structure encompasses nearly the complete protein (residues 38 to 95), and includes the NAC region (residues 61 to 95) of α-Syn.
source: In conclusion, we present the structure of recombinant α-Syn(1-121) fibrils determined at a resolution of 3.4 Å by cryo-EM. Our structure encompasses nearly the complete protein (residues 38 to 95), and includes the NAC region (residues 61 to 95) of α-Syn.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Various residues associated with familial forms of PD and other synucleinopathies are located in the interacting region between two protofilaments, suggesting their involvement in fibril formation and stabilization.
source: We determined that various residues associated with familial forms of PD and other synucleinopathies are located in the interacting region between two protofilaments, suggesting their involvement in fibril formation and stabilization.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure and inference about the role of these residues.

claim: The cryo-EM structure reveals how two protofilaments interact to form a fibril.
source: The cryo-EM structure presented here reveals how two protofilaments interact to form a fibril, and how the NAC region contributes to protofilament formation and stability.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The cryo-EM structure reveals how the NAC region contributes to protofilament formation and stability.
source: The cryo-EM structure presented here reveals how two protofilaments interact to form a fibril, and how the NAC region contributes to protofilament formation and stability.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure.

claim: In certain familial forms of PD, a different structure of α-Syn than this fibril strain might be involved.
source: Our structure also presents novel insights into how several PD-relevant mutations of α-Syn would compromise the structure of this fibril, suggesting that in the case of certain familial forms of PD, a different structure of α-Syn than this fibril strain might be involved.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural analysis of mutation sites.
